## KIMI K3: OPEN FRONTIER INTELLIGENCE

TECHNICAL REPORT OF KIMI K3

Kimi Team

## ABSTRACT

We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3 is built on Kimi Delta Attention [64] and Attention Residuals [58], which improve information flow across sequence length and model depth. Together with Stable LatentMoE, which effectively activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token, and refined training and data recipes, these advances yield an approximately  $ 2.5\times $ improvement in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2 [59]. Post-training highlights reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding domains and multiple reasoning-effort levels, enabling compositional generalization and robust long horizon execution. At 2.8T scale, Kimi K3 is supported by infrastructure advances in multiple areas: algorithm-system co-design for KDA, perfectly balanced expert-parallel training with efficient memory management, million-token agentic RL with persistent rollout and sandbox states, and deployment innovations.

## Processes to CUDA Threads

## Process

A running instance of a program, usually with its own address space.

## CPU Thread

An execution unit inside a process. Threads in the same process share memory.

## CUDA Thread

A lightweight execution unit running on the GPU.

Figure 4 GPU GRid block and Threads

## Key ideas

A thread is the basic execution unit of a CUDA kernel.

A block is a group of CUDA threads.

A grid is a group of thread blocks

threadIdx.x is the thread's x-coordinate within its block.

## Example

hello<<1, 4>>>();

1 block x 4 threads/block =4 CUDA threads

## Anatomy of a CUDA C++ Program iSingLab HKUST

## ○○○

#include <stdio.h>

#include <cuda_runtime.h>

## // CPU code int main()

// 1. Prepare data on the CPU

// 2. Allocate memory on the GPU

cudaMalloc(...);

// 3. Copy input data from CPU to GPU

cudaMemcpy(...);

// 4. Launch the CUDA kernel

kernel<<<...>>>(...);

// 5. Wait for the GPU to finish

cudaDeviceSynchronize();

// 6. Copy results from GPU to CPU

cudaMemcpy(...);

// 7. Free GPU memory

cudaFree(...);

return 0;

### Two Parts in One .cu File

GPU / Device Code

□ Defines the CUDA kernel

Executed on the GPU

Run by many CUDA threads

CPU / Host Code

□ Prepares input data

□ Manages GPU memory

Transfers data between CPU and GPU

Launches the CUDA kernel

Collects the results

A CUDA C++ program contains both CPU code and GPU code.

<!-- page: 16 -->

// CPU code

int main()

{

    // 1. Prepare data on the CPU No input data is needed in this simple example

    printf("Hello from CPU!\\n");

    // 2. Allocate memory on the GPU Not needed because there is no in/output array

    // 3. Copy input data from CPU to GPUNot needed because there is no input data

    // 4. Launch the CUDA kernel 1 block, 4 CUDA threads

    hello<<1, 4>>();

    // 5. Wait for the GPU to finish

    cudaDeviceSynchronize();

    // 6. Copy results from GPU to CPU Not needed because there is no output data

    // 7. Free GPU memory Not needed because no GPU memory was allocated.

    return 0;

}

## Kernel Launch and Device printf

## ○○○

#include <stdio.h>

#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// GPU code CUDA kernel executed on the GPU

__global__ void hello()

{

    // Each CUDA thread executes this once

    printf("Hello from GPU! Thread %d\n", threadIdx.x);

}

{

}

// 1. Prepare data on the CPU

int A[N] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8};

int B[N] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80};

int C[N] = {0};

int *d_A;

int *d_B;

int *d_C;

int bytes = N * sizeof(int);

// 2. Allocate memory on the GPU

cudaMalloc((void**)&d_A, bytes);

cudaMalloc((void**)&d_B, bytes);

cudaMalloc((void**)&d_C, bytes);





Allocate GPU memory

(d_A, d_B, d_C)

// 3. Copy input data from CPU to GPU

cudaMemcpy(d_A, A, bytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice)

cudaMemcpy(d_B, B, bytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice)

2 Copy A, B to GPU

 $ (A \rightarrow d_A, B \rightarrow d_B) $



// 4. Launch the CUDA kernel

int threadsPerBlock = 4;

int blocks = (N + threadsPerBlock - 1) / threadsPerBlock;

vectorAdd<<blocks, threadsPerBlock>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, N);

// 5. Wait for the GPU to finish

cudaDeviceSynchronize();

// 6. Copy results from GPU to CPU

cudaMemcpy(C, d_C, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost)

Figure 9 The Transformer model architecture

 $$ S_{i,j}^{^{\prime}}=S_{i,j}+M_{i,j} $$ 

 $$ S,M,S^{^{\prime}}\;\in\;\left(\mathbb{R}\;\cup\left\{\pm\infty\right\}\right)^{L\times L} $$ 

L: sequence length

S: attention score matrix

M: attention mask

 $$ \begin{bmatrix}s_{00}&s_{01}&s_{02}&s_{03}\\ s_{10}&s_{11}&s_{12}&s_{13}\\ s_{20}&s_{21}&s_{22}&s_{23}\\ s_{30}&s_{31}&s_{32}&s_{33}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0&-\infty&-\infty&-\infty\\ 0&0&-\infty&-\infty\\ 0&0&0&-\infty\\ 0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix} $$ 

 $$ \begin{aligned}=\begin{bmatrix}S_{00}&-\infty&-\infty&-\infty\\S_{10}&S_{11}&-\infty&-\infty\\S_{20}&S_{21}&S_{22}&-\infty\\S_{30}&S_{31}&S_{32}&S_{33}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ 

The same operation is applied independently to every  $ (row, col) $.

## 2 D CUDA Kernel for Addition

## ○○○

_global__ void addMask(const float *S, const float *M, float *out, int rows, int cols)

// 1. Find my row

int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;

// 2. Find my column

int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

// 3. Check whether this matrix element exists

if (row < rows && col < cols)

{

    // 4. Convert (row, col) to a linear memory index

    int index = row * cols + col;

    // 5. Compute one output element

    out[index] = S[index] + M[index];

}

CUDA thread

blockIdx + threadIdx

(row, col)

linear index

row * cols + col

one output

out[index]

(blockIdx.x, threadIdx.x)

(blockIdx.y, threadIdx.y)

(row, col)

index

## 2 D Matrix Multiplication

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_20_244_758_1302.jpg" alt="Image" width="36%" /></div>


Figure 9 The Transformer

model architecture

 $$ Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V $$ 

 $$ Q=\begin{bmatrix}q_{11}&q_{12}&\cdots&q_{1d_{k}}\\ q_{21}&q_{22}&\cdots&q_{2d_{k}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ q_{L1}&q_{L2}&\cdots&q_{L d_{k}}\end{bmatrix},\quad K^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}k_{11}&k_{21}&\cdots&k_{L1}\\ k_{12}&k_{22}&\cdots&k_{L2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ k_{1d_{k}}&k_{2d_{k}}&\cdots&k_{L d_{k}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times L} $$ 

 $$ S=Q K^{\top}=\left[\begin{matrix}{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{1r}k_{1r}}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{1r}k_{2r}}&{\cdots}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{1r}k_{L r}}\\ {\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{2r}k_{1r}}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{2r}k_{2r}}&{\cdots}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{2r}k_{L r}}\\ {\vdots}&{\vdots}&{\ddots}&{\vdots}\\ {\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{L r}k_{1r}}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{L r}k_{2r}}&{\cdots}&{\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{L r}k_{L r}}\\ \end{matrix}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L} $$ 

 $$ \begin{aligned}S_{ij}&=Q_{i,:}K_{j,:}^{T}=[q_{i1}\quad q_{i2}\quad\cdots\quad q_{id_{k}}]\begin{bmatrix}k_{j1}\\ k_{j2}\\ \vdots\\ k_{jd_{k}}\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{ir}k_{jr}\in\mathbb{R}\\ Matrix\ Multiplication\end{aligned} $$ 

 $$ (i,j)\mapsto S_{i j}=\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}Q_{i r}K_{j r} $$ 

 $$ \boxed{C\leftarrow\alpha A B+\beta C} $$

## Standard block multiplication

 $$ \boldsymbol{A}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\ A_{21}&A_{22}\end{bmatrix} $$ 

 $$ \boldsymbol{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{B}_{11}&\boldsymbol{B}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{B}_{21}&\boldsymbol{B}_{22}\end{bmatrix}, $$ 

 $$ \boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}=\begin{bmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\ C_{21}&C_{22}\end{bmatrix} $$ 

 $$ C_{11}~=~A_{11}B_{11}~+~A_{12}B_{21} $$ 

 $$ C_{12}=A_{11}B_{12}+A_{12}B_{22} $$ 

 $$ C_{21}~=~A_{21}B_{11}~+~A_{22}B_{21} $$ 

 $$ C_{22}~=~A_{21}B_{12}~+~A_{22}B_{22} $$ 

Needs 8 block multiplications + 4 block additions

 $$ \Theta(N^{3}) $$ 

Less expensive multiplications

## Strassen's idea

1969

Seven intermediate products (only 7 block multiplications):

 $$ M_{1}=(A_{11}+A_{22})(B_{11}+B_{22}) $$ 

 $$ M_{2}=(A_{21}+A_{22})B_{11} $$ 

 $$ M_{3}=A_{11}(B_{12}-B_{22}) $$ 

 $$ M_{4}\quad=\quad A_{22}(B_{21}-B_{11}) $$ 

 $$ M_{5}~=~(A_{11}+A_{12})B_{22} $$ 

 $$ M_{6}~=~(A_{21}-A_{11})(B_{11}+B_{12}) $$ 

 $$ M_{7}~=~(A_{12}-A_{22})(B_{21}+B_{22}) $$ 

Recombine to get the blocks of C = AB:

 $$ C_{11}~=~M_{1}+M_{4}-M_{5}+M_{7} $$ 

 $$ C_{12}~=~M_{3}+M_{5} $$ 

 $$ C_{21}~=~M_{2}+M_{4} $$ 

 $$ C_{22}=M_{1}-M_{2}+M_{3}+M_{6} $$ 

Needs 7 block multiplications + more additions/subtractions

 $$ \theta(n^{l o g_{2}^{7}})=\theta(n^{2.807}) $$ 

More cheaper addition

 $$ \begin{bmatrix}4&0&4&0&3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\ 0\\ 5\\ 0\\ 5\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. \quad = ? $$ 

 $$ 4\times4+0\times0+4\times5+0\times0+3\times5+0\times0=51 $$ 

6 multiplications + 5 additions

 $$ 4\times4+4\times5+3\times5=51 $$ 

3 multiplications + 2 additions FASTER

1. Sparse matrix

 $$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}0&0&4&0&0\\0&0&0&0&-2\\3&0&0&0&0\\0&0&0&5&0\\0&1&0&0&0\end{array}\right] $$ 

## Most entries are zero

Only a small fraction are nonzero (e.g., 5 nonzeros out of 25 entries = 20%)

Dense view: store every entry.

Sparse view: store only nonzero values + positions.

### 2. Special storage formats

Coordinate format (COO)

Store a list of (row, column, value) for each nonzero.

### 3. Special computation

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication: y = Ax

 $$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{c c c c c}{0}&{0}&{4}&{0}&{0}\\ {0}&{0}&{0}&{0}&{-2}\\ {3}&{0}&{0}&{0}&{0}\\ {0}&{0}&{0}&{5}&{0}\\ {0}&{1}&{0}&{0}&{0}\end{array}\right]\quad\boldsymbol{x}=\left[\begin{array}{l}{x_{1}}\\ {x_{2}}\\ {x_{3}}\\ {x_{4}}\\ {x_{5}}\end{array}\right]\Longrightarrow\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{l}{y_{1}}\\ {y_{2}}\\ {y_{3}}\\ {y_{4}}\\ {y_{5}}\end{array}\right] $$ 

Skip multiplications by zero (use only nonzeros)

Fewer memory accesses

Common kernels: SpMV (A x), SpMM (A B)

Performance depends on sparsity pattern and memory access regularity.
